t.1.8.1: The Sūta said: And that Cyavana too, the Bhārgava, O brahmin, begot upon Sukanyā a son, the great-souled Pramati of blazing splendor.
t.1.8.2: Pramati begot on Ghṛtācī a son named Ruru, and Ruru begot Śunaka on Pramadvarā.
t.1.8.3: O brahmin, I shall relate in detail the entire story of that Ruru of abundant splendor; listen to it, all of it, without omission.
t.1.8.4: Long ago there was a great seer endowed with austerity and learning, known as Sthūlakeśa, who delighted in the welfare of all beings.
t.1.8.6: Then, O joy of the Bhṛgus, that apsaras Menakā, when her time had come, abandoned that offspring near the hermitage of Sthūlakeśa.
t.1.8.5: At that very time, O brahmin seer, the king of the Gandharvas, renowned as Viśvāvasu, begot a child upon Menakā.
t.1.8.8: The great and glorious ṛṣi Sthūlakeśa saw her abandoned on the bank of a river, in a lonely place, bereft of kinsmen.
t.1.8.7: Having abandoned that offspring on the bank of the river, the maiden who resembled a child of the immortals and seemed to blaze with beauty, she went away.
t.1.8.9: Then Sthūlakeśa, the best of the twice-born, saw that girl, and that foremost of sages, filled with compassion, took her up and nourished her. And the fair-hipped, lovely girl grew up in his hermitage.
t.1.8.10: She, endowed with every beauty and virtue, was the most excellent of women; therefore the great seer gave her the name Pramadvarā.
t.1.8.11: Having seen that Pramadvarā in his hermitage, the righteous-souled Ruru, so it is said, became one whose heart was possessed by love.
t.1.8.12: Then that Bhārgava had his father told of it through his friends, and Pramati, having heard, went to the illustrious Sthūlakeśa.
t.1.8.13: Then the father gave that maiden, Pramadvarā, to Ruru, having first set the wedding under the lunar mansion whose presiding deity is Bhaga.
t.1.8.14: Then, when the wedding was only a few days away, that maiden of lovely complexion was playing together with her friends.
t.1.8.15: She did not see the snake lying asleep, stretched out across her path, and, impelled by Time and destined to die, she trod upon it with her foot.
t.1.8.16: Impelled by the law of Time, he violently sank his poison-smeared fangs into the body of that heedless girl.
t.1.8.17: Bitten, she suddenly fell to the ground, senseless and lifeless; though now unfit to be looked upon, her form was still most lovely to behold.
t.1.8.18: Stricken by the snake's venom, she lay upon the ground as though fast asleep, and the slender-waisted maiden became even more enchanting than before.
t.1.8.20: Then all the foremost of the twice-born, filled with compassion, came together: Svastyātreya, Mahājānu, Kuśika, and Śaṅkhamekhala.
t.1.8.19: Her father saw her, and so too did those other ascetics: she who shone like a lotus, fallen on the ground and writhing.
t.1.8.22: Seeing that maiden lifeless, stricken by the serpent's venom, they wept, overcome with pity; but Ruru, deeply distressed, went outside.
t.1.8.21: Bhāradvāja, Kauṇakutsa, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and then Gautama, Pramati together with his son, and likewise other forest-dwellers came.
